prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene satisfies what I look for in a discovery prize. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model made a sharp, falsifiable prediction in 2011, and in 2018 the Jarillo-Herrero group observed correlated insulating and superconducting states at the predicted angle. That is the original experiment, not a later and more elegant one. It also opened a door: a clean, electrostatically tunable platform where interactions, band topology and superconductivity can be varied in one device, which people could not do before. Independent groups have reproduced the core phenomena in twisted bilayer graphene and in several other moire systems, so the experimental verification the Nobel mandate requires is in place. The theory-plus-experiment trio maps onto the named people without needing a fourth name.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The field is only about eight years old, and the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so a skeptic can say we are rewarding a promising platform before we understand it. On attribution, the 2018 experiments were carried out by a team in which Yuan Cao was a lead author, and the Dean group's contemporaneous moire work and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto could be raised. The three-person limit then looks tight. If the committee decides the history is not clean enough, or that it wants a more settled field, the optical lattice clock is the better-established alternative.

responses.point: Ulf ranks the quantum spin Hall / topological insulator discovery first and proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, while rating magic-angle graphene as strong but borderline on timing because the field is only about eight years old and the superconducting mechanism is debated.
responses.response: I agree the pairing mechanism is open, but I do not think the prize requires a settled mechanism. It requires an original, verified observation, and the correlated insulators and superconducting domes have been reproduced widely. On B053 I share your view that it is a strong discovery, but I put Hasan in place of Mele because the 3D ARPES work is a separate, decisive experiment, and I do not see how a three-name award avoids leaving out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu. Your Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is theory-heavy with one experiment, and it leaves the 3D discovery unrecognised. That attribution problem is, for me, a larger obstacle than the age of the moire field.

responses.point: Mark places the IceCube astrophysical neutrino discovery first, as an instrument-driven opening of a new window, and proposes Halzen and Karle. He puts optical clocks second and magic-angle graphene third, noting that the pairing is not settled and the work may be somewhat early.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument; it is close to my own bias for tools that open doors. But I put IceCube sixth, for two reasons. First, I cannot be absolutely sure that three names capture who did the original work in a collaboration of this size with the AMANDA and Baikal precursors. You yourself note that the allocation between Halzen, Karle and Spiering is not unique and propose only two. Second, source identification is still partial. By contrast the moire discovery was made by one identifiable group, with a theory prediction that preceded it by seven years. I accept your point on maturity, and that is the main reason I keep the clock as my first alternative.

responses.point: Stefan ranks the optical lattice clock first, as measurement-limited progress that opened relativistic geodesy, tests of varying constants and a redefinition of the second, with Katori and Ye as a clean pair.
responses.response: I agree that Katori and Ye is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that the clocks are thoroughly reproduced; I ranked it third and it is my first alternative. My qualification is about the original-experiment test. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is the original idea, but the record-setting performance came through a process in which several groups, including Lemonde, Gill and the NIST teams, contributed, and Hall and Haensch were honoured in 2005 for the comb on which these clocks depend. A new measurement tool is a legitimate prize, and I would not object to it, but moire matter opened more physics that could not be seen before.

responses.point: Olle ranks magic-angle graphene first as a materials discovery where theory and experiment are tightly linked, and ranks the topological insulator candidate second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, valuing Hasan's ARPES work.
responses.response: We agree on both the first choice and the Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan trio for B053, and I share your point that spectroscopy-linked experiments are the kind of verification I weigh. I would add a caution to my own position and to yours: with Mele left out of this trio, the allocation is hard to defend as the original theory credit. If the committee ends up on B053, I would want the record of Kane-Mele versus Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang checked closely before we commit.

uncertainties: Whether the 2018 experimental credit is adequately captured by Jarillo-Herrero alone, given that Yuan Cao and the Dean group's work on related moire systems fall outside the credited names.
Whether the committee regards a field about eight years old, with an unsettled superconducting mechanism, as mature enough.
Whether prior theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto weakens the Bistritzer-MacDonald priority claim.
Whether a theory-plus-experiment pairing in condensed matter is preferable to the cleaner two-person optical clock configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B015 from my profile. I do have a disciplinary connection to B048 (aberration-corrected TEM), because I work in electron microscopy, and I would recuse myself from deciding that candidate, which is not in my preferred configuration. I have no direct tie to Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald or Bistritzer, though I note that the committee colleague Goran Johansson shares my Chalmers department.
